newsitem.title: UK: Investment banking on trial after NatWest.
newsitem.headline: Investment banking on trial after NatWest.

text.p: With blood on the carpet at NatWest Markets, the investment banking arm of National Westminster Bank Plc, the question was again being asked on Monday: Can British banks ever succeed in competition with Wall Street firms?
The flag for these aspirations is currently only being carried by NatWest and by Barclays Plc in the shape of its investment bank BZW.

Other British investment banks have fallen prey to foreign predators, most notably S.G. Warburg, the most thrusting of the breed during the 1980s, which found it impossible to compete with the "bulge-bracket" and was taken over by Swiss Bank Corp in 1995 after an ignominious failure when it tried to merge with Morgan Stanley.

City of London analysts complain that Barclays and NatWest continue to pour capital into their investment banking forays and are willing to see the poor returns that this means for the group as a whole when compared to groups such as Lloyds TSB which focus on retail banking.

Panmure Gordon analyst David Poutney recently described NatWest's credibility gap in the stock market as "cavernous" as he trimmed his 1997 profit forecast, adding that the bank had underperformed the sector for a decade.
Now there are signs that NatWest has got the message from the market.

Monday's statement by the bank announcing the resignation of NatWest Markets chief executive Martin Owen and appointing group chief Derek Wanless in his place, shows that NatWest is looking to curb its aspirations to be a global player.

"Our focus will be on areas where we have a competitive advantage with a strong product or research base and high quality people," said Wanless in a statement, "deploying capital in those ...activities where better returns can be achieved."
Analysts have said that NatWest must remove itself from capital intensive, low-margin business such as corporate lending where margins have been as thin as cigarette paper.

In a business where reputation is so important, NatWest Market's 90 million pounds loss in options trading, announced in February, has had a big knock-on effect to the extent that NatWest posted a profits warning for the first half of this year. The bank said pre-tax profits for the first half of 1997 would not exceed 770 million pounds, a warning which saw NatWest shares dive 41-1/2p to 755. Owen seems to have underestimated the effect of the options loss, saying at the time that the loss had holed the investment bank "above the water line." Now, it seems clear that the hole was well below and water has been gushing in.
Where does all this leave BZW?

After its disastrous performance in 1996, when profits slumped by 26 percent, rumours have been rife that Barclays chief executive Martin Taylor has made it clear to BZW chief Bill Harrison that things must improve.

There has been much discussion over whether BZW might be sold or scaled down although Taylor has insisted that it is not for sale and sources close to the bank say that Harrison is being given time to improve returns.
Taylor has said that investment will continue but that, after the disruption of a change in offices, he expects BZW's performance to be "a lot better" in the second half of 1997.
BZW has followed a different path to NatWest, with fewer acquisitions but, for example, is very short of capacity in US dollar markets.
As integrated banks, NatWest Markets and BZW would be difficult to sell, as much of their revenue stems from the customer base in the group.
Analysts doubt their ability, however, to compete in the top bracket which looks set to consolidate even further in the next few years.

"It could be that both firms finally come to the conclusion that investment must be curbed," said one analyst. "Where do you draw the line if you keep investing to improve returns but the returns never improve?"
